resources.string: What is it for?
your code
processor
You write total equals price plus two. The processor can't read that.
Which of the two does the processor understand? Tap it.
It only reads short instructions, like load, add and store.
Right. Machine code. Your code has to turn into that.
Translating it all at once would be hard and full of mistakes.
So the compiler splits the work into six phases, one after the other.
Then comes intermediate code: one operation per line, easy to translate.
Optimization removes what's extra. Generation writes the machine code.
What comes out of each phase
The recipe is what comes out of each phase. It stays here on screen.
Lexical → tokens
Syntactic → tree
Semantic → tree with types
Intermediate → one operation per line
Optimization → fewer operations
Generation → machine code
A spelling mistake belongs to the lexical phase. A shape mistake belongs to the syntactic one.
A meaning mistake, like a mixed-up type, belongs to the semantic phase.
Another piece of code
Now this while goes through the same phases.
Who cuts the while into tokens? Tap the phase.
It's the first phase. It only looks at the letters.
Right. The lexical phase cuts and names each piece.
If the closing parenthesis is missing, which phase complains?
The letters are fine. What's missing is the shape of the statement.
Right. A parenthesis without its pair breaks the tree. That's syntactic.
In which phase does the loop turn into jumps, one operation per line?
It comes after the semantic phase and before optimization.
Right. Intermediate code writes the loop with jumps.
Six phases in order. The game map follows this same path.
The parser has T on top and reads id. T has two rules.
It only picks right if it knows what each rule starts with.
The tokens that can start a symbol form its FIRST.
In this grammar, each symbol gets a bag for its FIRST.
FIRST recipe
The FIRST recipe has three rules. It stays here on screen.
1. Terminal at the start: it goes in.
2. Nonterminal at the start: its FIRST.
3. Can vanish: look at the next symbol.
Rule one: if the rule starts with a terminal, it goes in.
In E goes to T X, which rule of the recipe do you use? Tap it.
E starts with T, and T has rules of its own.
Right. Rule two: the FIRST of T goes into the FIRST of E.
Rule three: if that symbol can vanish, look at the next one too.
Another grammar. Now you do the math, with the recipe.
A starts with a, or vanishes. Tap what goes into the FIRST of A.
One rule starts with the terminal a. The other is epsilon.
Right. Both go into the FIRST of A.
S goes to A b, and A can vanish. Which token also starts S?
If A vanishes, the b ends up at the start.
Right. By rule three, the b goes in.
The other rule of S is still missing. Tap what goes in through it.
The second rule of S starts with a terminal.
Right. The letter c goes in by rule one.
FIRST of S: a, b and c. Now the parser knows which rule to pick.
The parser has X on top and reads a closing parenthesis. X can vanish.
Erasing X only makes sense if a closing parenthesis can come after X.
What can come right after a symbol forms its FOLLOW.
Three bags again. Now for what comes after.
FOLLOW recipe
The FOLLOW recipe also has three rules.
1. The start symbol gets the dollar sign.
2. After B comes β: the FIRST of β goes in.
3. β can vanish: B inherits the parent's FOLLOW.
Rule one: the start symbol gets the dollar sign.
The plus from the FIRST of X went into the FOLLOW of T. Which rule did that?
X comes right after T. It's the FIRST of what comes after.
Right. Rule two.
Rule three: if the rest can vanish, the symbol inherits the parent's FOLLOW.
Now a bigger grammar. The goal is the FOLLOW of F.
In T goes to F Y, Y comes after F. Which token does Y start with?
Look at Y's rule. What comes before the F?
Right. The times goes in by rule two.
Y can vanish. So F inherits whose FOLLOW? Tap it.
F is inside T's rule.
Right. By rule three, everything that follows T also follows F.
The FOLLOW of T has plus, closing parenthesis and dollar sign. All of it goes down to F.
FOLLOW of F: times, plus, closing parenthesis and dollar sign.
